content: Bacillus is a genus of bacteria characterized by its rod-shaped structure and Gram-positive staining properties. These bacteria belong to the division Firmicutes. Members of the Bacillus genus can be either obligate aerobes, requiring oxygen for survival, or facultative aerobes, capable of surviving with or without oxygen. They test positive for the enzyme catalase, which helps them break down hydrogen peroxide. Bacillus species are widely distributed in nature and include both free-living and pathogenic organisms. Under harsh environmental conditions, Bacillus cells can form oval-shaped endospores, which allow them to remain dormant for long periods. While these features were initially used to define the genus, not all species with these traits are closely related, and some have been reclassified into other genera. One of the most well-studied species within this genus is Bacillus subtilis. This bacterium has been extensively researched in molecular and cellular biology due to its genetic accessibility and relatively large size, which make it an excellent model organism. Advances in fluorescence microscopy have provided remarkable insights into the dynamic structure of this single-celled organism. Research on Bacillus subtilis has significantly contributed to our understanding of bacterial differentiation, gene and protein regulation, and cell cycle processes. Two species of Bacillus are of particular medical importance. Bacillus anthracis is the causative agent of anthrax, a serious infectious disease, while Bacillus cereus is associated with foodborne illnesses that resemble those caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Another species, Bacillus thuringiensis, is an insect pathogen and is often used as a biological control agent to manage insect pests. The type species of the genus, Bacillus subtilis, is not only a key model organism but also a known food spoiler, causing a condition called ropiness in bread and similar foods. Bacillus coagulans is another species implicated in food spoilage. To isolate Bacillus species, a simple method involves placing non-sterile soil in a test tube with water, shaking it, and then transferring the mixture to melted Mannitol Salt Agar. After incubation at room temperature for at least 24 hours, colonies typically appear large, spreading, and irregularly shaped. Under a microscope, Bacillus cells are observed as rod-shaped structures, often containing an oval endospore at one end, which causes the cell to bulge. The cell wall is primarily composed of peptidoglycan, along with teichoic and teichuronic acids. Bacillus subtilis was the first bacterium in which the role of an actin-like cytoskeleton in determining cell shape and directing peptidoglycan synthesis was identified. Additionally, the complete set of enzymes involved in peptidoglycan synthesis has been localized in this species. The cytoskeleton plays a critical role in maintaining the shape and structural integrity of the cell. It is important to note that the term Bacillus, when capitalized and italicized, specifically refers to the genus. However, the lowercase term bacillus is a general descriptor for any rod-shaped bacterium, regardless of its taxonomic classification. Rod-shaped bacteria, or bacilli, are found across various bacterial groups. Additionally, Bacilli (capitalized) refers to the class to which the Bacillus genus belongs, while bacilli (lowercase) is a morphological term. It is also worth mentioning that the term bacillus does not necessarily imply Gram-positive staining, as some rod-shaped bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, are Gram-negative.
